questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: C.2 (Wave model: reflection, refraction, superposition, interference, polarisation)
questions.challenge_mechanism: Four of the five keys require a distinction that students routinely collapse: field strength cancels at the midpoint between two masses but potential does not, intensity is the square of the sum of amplitudes rather than the sum of squares, and the interior field of a uniform sphere rises linearly rather than following the inverse-square law.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions on the wave model. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Unless a question says otherwise, the frequency of a wave is fixed by its source and does not change when the wave crosses a boundary between two media.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A transverse pulse travels along a stretched string whose far end is rigidly clamped. What happens to the pulse when it reaches the clamped end?

options.label: A
options.rationale: A fixed end cannot move, so the incident and reflected displacements must cancel there, which requires the reflected pulse to be inverted relative to the incident one.

options.label: B
options.text: It is reflected without being inverted.
options.rationale: An unchanged reflection happens at a free end, where the string is able to move; a clamped end imposes the opposite boundary condition.

options.label: C
options.text: It passes into the support without reflection.
options.rationale: The clamp is a boundary between media of very different impedance, so almost all of the pulse energy is reflected rather than transmitted.

options.label: D
options.text: It is inverted only if the pulse amplitude is large enough.
options.rationale: Inversion follows from the boundary condition and not from the amplitude, so it happens for a pulse of any size.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A water wave of frequency $2.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$ travels from deep water, where its speed is $0.80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, into shallow water, where its speed is $0.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What happens to its wavelength?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The frequency is unchanged across the boundary at $2.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so the wavelength is speed divided by frequency: $0.80/2.0=0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ becomes $0.60/2.0=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This has the change in the right direction but the wrong starting values, as though the wave were travelling from shallow water into deep.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This keeps the wavelength fixed across the boundary, confusing wavelength with frequency, which is the quantity that does stay fixed.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This scales the wavelength by the ratio of the speeds a second time, as though the frequency changed as well as the speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Two coherent sources emit in phase. At a point P the difference in the distances from the two sources to P is $1.5\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength. What is observed at P?

options.label: A
options.text: A minimum, because the path difference is an odd number of half-wavelengths.
options.rationale: A path difference of $1.5\lambda$ is three half-wavelengths, an odd number, which corresponds to a phase difference of $540^{\circ}$, equivalent to $180^{\circ}$, so the arrivals cancel.

options.label: B
options.text: A maximum, because the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.
options.rationale: One and a half is not a whole number of wavelengths, so the two arrivals are not in phase and cannot reinforce.

options.label: C
options.text: A maximum, because the path difference corresponds to a phase difference of $180^{\circ}$.
options.rationale: The phase difference is stated correctly but the conclusion is inverted; a $180^{\circ}$ phase difference is precisely the condition for cancellation.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither a maximum nor a minimum, because the condition only applies when the path difference is zero.
options.rationale: Both maxima and minima occur at non-zero path differences, at whole wavelengths and odd half-wavelengths respectively.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Two coherent waves of amplitudes $3A$ and $A$ superpose in phase. What is the ratio of the intensity of the resultant wave to the intensity of the larger wave on its own?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Amplitudes add first, giving a resultant of $4A$, and intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so the ratio is $16A^{2}/9A^{2}=16/9=1.78$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This takes the ratio of the amplitudes rather than of the intensities, forgetting to square before comparing.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This adds the two intensities as though the waves were incoherent, which discards the interference term that dominates here.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This squares the resultant amplitude but forgets to divide by the intensity of the larger wave, so it is not a ratio.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_{0}$ is incident on a polariser. A second polariser, whose transmission axis is at $60^{\circ}$ to the first, is placed after it. What is the intensity of the light emerging from the second polariser?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The first polariser halves the unpolarised intensity to $I_{0}/2$ and the second applies Malus' law, multiplying by the square of the cosine of $60^{\circ}$, giving $0.5\times0.25=0.125\,I_{0}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This applies Malus' law but forgets that the first polariser halves the intensity of the unpolarised beam before the second one acts.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This uses the cosine of $60^{\circ}$ rather than its square, which Malus' law does not do, since intensity depends on the square of the field amplitude.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This appears to treat the angle as reducing the intensity by a simple factor of one minus the cosine, which has no basis in Malus' law.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** A clamped end is a fixed boundary: the displacement there must be zero at every instant, so the reflected pulse must cancel the incident one at that point, which means it is inverted. A free end gives an uninverted reflection instead. **(A1)** The distinction is the boundary condition, not the size of the pulse.

**(b) A.** Frequency is set by the source and is unchanged on crossing the boundary. With $v=f\lambda$, the deep-water wavelength is $0.80/2.0=0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ and the shallow-water wavelength is $0.60/2.0=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. **(A1)** C is the common error: it is the frequency that is invariant, not the wavelength.

**(c) A.** A path difference of $1.5\lambda$ equals three half-wavelengths, an odd number, so the phase difference is $3\pi$ radians, equivalent to $\pi$, and the superposing arrivals cancel. **(A1)** C is the trap worth noting: it names the correct phase difference and then draws the opposite conclusion.

**(d) A.** Amplitudes add before squaring: the resultant is $3A+A=4A$, so the resultant intensity is proportional to $16A^{2}$ while the larger wave alone is proportional to $9A^{2}$, giving $16/9=1.78$. **(A1)** B omits the squaring and C treats the waves as incoherent, which would give $(9+1)/9=1.11$ and would be right only if the phase relationship were random.

**(e) A.** The first polariser transmits half the unpolarised intensity, giving $I_{0}/2$ of plane-polarised light. Malus' law then multiplies by $\cos^{2}60^{\circ}=0.25$, so the final intensity is $I_{0}/2\times0.25=0.125\,I_{0}$. **(A1)** B, at $0.25\,I_{0}$, is Malus' law applied without the initial halving.
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept any statement that the pulse is reflected and inverted; a candidate who adds that the reflection at a free end is not inverted shows the contrasting case and should not be penalised for the extra material. (b) Accept $0.40$ and $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$; the mark is for holding the frequency constant, so a candidate who changes the frequency and gets both wavelengths wrong earns nothing. (c) Accept any justification in terms of an odd number of half-wavelengths; note that $1.5\lambda$ and $2.5\lambda$ give the same verdict, so the answer does not depend on which odd multiple was chosen. (d) Accept $1.7$ to $1.8$, or the exact fraction $16/9$; a candidate who writes $16$ has done the hard part and then omitted the division, and should be given the benefit of the doubt only if the ratio was clearly intended. (e) Accept $0.125$ or $I_{0}/8$; the two-stage structure is the point, so a single-stage answer earns nothing.
questions.explanation:
This cluster tests the wave model through a series of distinctions that are easy to state and easy to forget under pressure. In (a) the boundary condition decides the reflection, and a fixed end is not a free end. In (b) exactly one of frequency and wavelength is invariant across a boundary, and it is the one students are least inclined to hold constant because they can see the wavelength change. In (c) the classification depends on whether the path difference is an odd or an even number of half-wavelengths, and the $1.5\lambda$ value is chosen so that the wrong counting gives a confident wrong answer.

Items (d) and (e) are where the cluster earns its difficulty, because both hinge on an operation that must be done before the comparison. In (d) amplitudes must be added first and only then squared, because intensity is proportional to the square of the resultant amplitude; adding the intensities instead throws away the cross term, which is the entire interference effect and is larger than one of the two intensities on its own. In (e) there are two stages and the first is the one that gets forgotten: unpolarised light loses half its intensity at the first polariser, and Malus' law applies only to the polarised beam that emerges. Both items reward a candidate who writes down what is being combined before reaching for a formula, and both punish one who pattern-matches the surface features of the question.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. Distractors were built from the inversions and omissions characteristic of this subtopic: free-end boundary condition applied at a fixed end, wavelength held constant across a boundary, intensities added instead of amplitudes, and Malus' law applied without the initial halving.

verification.method: Every key and every distractor recomputed in Python to full precision; each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error rather than a nearby number.
solution_skeleton: apply the boundary condition at the end of the medium to decide whether a pulse inverts
hold the frequency constant across a boundary and recompute the wavelength from the new speed
convert the path difference into a count of half-wavelengths to classify the interference
add the amplitudes first and square the resultant when comparing intensities
apply the halving at the first polariser and then Malus' law at the second

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: D.1 (Gravitational fields: potential, field strength, escape speed, orbital energy)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The discriminating step in four of the five items is a distinction that looks like a detail and is not: potential adds where field strength cancels, orbital energy is half the potential energy and negative, escape speed depends on the square root of the distance rather than the distance, and the field inside a uniform sphere rises linearly with radius rather than falling as the inverse square.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions on gravitational fields. Each one stands alone. The gravitational potential is taken to be zero at infinity throughout, so the potential at any finite distance from a mass is negative. $G$ is the gravitational constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two point masses, each of mass $M$, are separated by a distance $2d$. What is the gravitational potential at the midpoint between them?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Potential is a scalar, so the two contributions add: each mass is a distance $d$ away and contributes $-GM/d$, giving a total of $-2GM/d$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This treats the potential as though it cancelled like the field strength, but potential is a scalar and the two negative contributions add rather than oppose.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This counts only one of the two masses, ignoring that potentials from separate sources always superpose by simple addition.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The magnitude and the addition are right but the sign is wrong; with the potential zero at infinity it is negative everywhere near a mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The escape speed from the surface of a planet of radius $R$ is $v$. What is the escape speed from a point at a distance $2R$ from the centre of the same planet?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Escape speed is the square root of $2GM/r$, so doubling the distance from the centre divides the speed by the square root of two, giving $0.707\,v$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This treats the escape speed as inversely proportional to distance, missing the square root that comes from equating kinetic energy to the potential well depth.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This has the square root the right way up but points the change in the wrong direction, as though moving outwards made escape harder.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This treats escape speed as a property of the planet alone, whereas it depends on the distance from the centre at which the escaping body starts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A satellite of mass $m$ is in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around a planet of mass $M$. What is the total energy of the satellite?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The potential energy is $-GMm/r$ and the kinetic energy is half that magnitude and positive, so the total is $-GMm/r + GMm/(2r) = -GMm/(2r)$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the gravitational potential energy alone and omits the kinetic energy the satellite has by virtue of being in orbit.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the kinetic energy on its own; the total is negative because a bound orbit has less energy than a stationary satellite at infinity.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Zero total energy corresponds to the borderline escape case, not to a closed circular orbit, which is bound and therefore has negative total energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius $R$ to a circular orbit of radius $2R$ around the same planet of mass $M$. What is the change in the total energy of the satellite?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The total energy is $-GMm/(2r)$, so it changes from $-GMm/(2R)$ to $-GMm/(4R)$, an increase of $GMm/(4R)$; energy must be supplied to lift the satellite outwards.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong; moving to a larger orbit makes the satellite less tightly bound, so its total energy rises towards zero.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This compares the magnitudes of the two total energies without taking their difference, so it double-counts the change.

options.label: D
options.text: No change, because the orbit is still circular.
options.rationale: The shape of the orbit does not fix its energy; a larger circular orbit has a different, less negative, total energy.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A planet of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has a uniform density. Let $g$ be the gravitational field strength at its surface. What is the gravitational field strength at a distance $R/2$ from its centre?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Inside a uniform sphere only the mass within the current radius contributes, and that mass falls as the cube of the radius, so the field rises linearly and at half the radius it is half the surface value.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This applies the inverse-square law inside the planet, as though the whole mass were still enclosed at the centre, which it is not.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This gets the direction of the change right but applies the inverse-square factor anyway, rather than the linear law that holds inside a uniform sphere.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Zero field at the centre is the correct result at $r=0$ for any spherical shell, but at half the radius there is still half the surface field.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** Gravitational potential is a scalar, so contributions add without any direction: each mass is a distance $d$ from the midpoint and contributes $-GM/d$, giving $-2GM/d$. **(A1)** Option B is the signature error of this subtopic, because it is the field strength that cancels at the midpoint by symmetry, not the potential.

**(b) A.** Equating kinetic energy to the depth of the potential well, $\tfrac12 mv_{e}^{2}=GMm/r$, gives $v_{e}=\sqrt{2GM/r}$. At $r=2R$ this is $\sqrt{2GM/(2R)}=v/\sqrt{2}=0.707\,v$. **(A1)** The square root is what B misses.

**(c) A.** For a circular orbit $\tfrac12 mv^{2}=GMm/(2r)$, so the kinetic energy is $+GMm/(2r)$ and the potential energy is $-GMm/r$; the total is $-GMm/(2r)$. **(A1)** The result is negative, which is the defining feature of a bound orbit, and the factor of two is the relationship students most often misremember.

**(d) A.** With $E=-GMm/(2r)$, the energy changes from $-GMm/(2R)$ to $-GMm/(4R)$. The change is $-GMm/(4R)-(-GMm/(2R))=+GMm/(4R)$, an increase. **(A1)** The sign is the point: raising an orbit requires an input of energy even though the satellite ends up moving more slowly.

**(e) A.** For a uniform sphere the enclosed mass within radius $r$ is $M r^{3}/R^{3}$, so $g(r)=G(Mr^{3}/R^{3})/r^{2}=GMr/R^{3}$, which rises linearly from zero at the centre to $g$ at the surface. At $r=R/2$ it is $g/2$. **(A1)** B is the inverse-square law applied where it does not hold.
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept $-2GM/d$; a candidate who explains that the field cancels while the potential does not has demonstrated the key idea even if the sign slips. (b) Accept $0.71\,v$ or $v/\sqrt{2}$; candidates often reach for the inverse-square law here, so credit should follow the square root rather than any particular rounding. (c) The negative sign is part of the answer and a positive magnitude alone does not earn the mark. (d) Accept the modulus with a clear statement of the direction; note the well-known paradox that the satellite slows down while gaining energy, and do not penalise a candidate who flags it. (e) Accept $g/2$ or $GM/(2R^{2})$; this item depends on the uniform-density assumption, which is stated in the stem, and a candidate who objects that real planets are not uniform is right but has not answered the question as set.
questions.explanation:
Gravitational fields are the subtopic where the most confident wrong answers come from applying a correct formula in the wrong regime, and this cluster is built almost entirely on that. In (e) the inverse-square law gives $4g$ at half the radius, which is badly wrong because inside a uniform sphere the enclosed mass falls faster than the distance does. In (b) the same instinct produces $0.500\,v$, because escape speed looks as though it should scale like the field strength, but the square root from the energy argument softens the dependence. In (a) the field strength and the potential behave in opposite ways at the midpoint between two equal masses, and the fact that one cancels while the other adds is the cleanest test of whether a student knows which is a vector.

The two orbital items, (c) and (d), probe the sign structure of orbital energy, which is the hardest part of the topic. A circular orbit has negative total energy, equal to half the potential energy, and moving outwards makes it less negative: the satellite gains energy and loses speed at the same time. That combination is counter-intuitive enough that a student who has only memorised the formula will often report the change in (d) with the wrong sign, and the $GMm/(2R)$ option is there for the candidate who compares magnitudes instead of taking a difference. Together the five items reward a student who checks which regime a formula belongs to before using it.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. Distractors were built from the regime and sign errors that dominate this subtopic: scalar potential treated as a vector, inverse-square law applied inside a mass distribution, potential energy quoted as total orbital energy, and a change in energy reported as a difference of magnitudes.

verification.method: Every key and every distractor recomputed in Python to full precision; each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error rather than a nearby number.
solution_skeleton: add the scalar potentials from each mass rather than cancelling them like field vectors
equate kinetic energy to the potential well depth and solve for the escape speed
combine the kinetic and potential terms to get the total orbital energy
take the difference of the total energies at the two orbital radii
use the enclosed mass inside a uniform sphere rather than the whole mass

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: D.3 (Motion in electromagnetic fields: charged particles in electric and magnetic fields)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, and almost every distractor in this cluster comes from forgetting one consequence of that: no work is done, so the speed is fixed, the period is independent of it, and the radius has to be expressed in terms of whichever quantity the question actually holds constant.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions on the motion of charged particles in electromagnetic fields. Each one stands alone. Unless a question states otherwise, any magnetic field is uniform and the particle enters it travelling at right angles to the field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field. Which statement about the particle is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The direction of its velocity changes but the magnitude does not.
options.rationale: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes the direction of motion without doing any work and therefore leaves the speed unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Both the direction and the magnitude of its velocity change.
options.rationale: This would require the force to have a component along the velocity, which the magnetic force never does, since it is perpendicular by construction.

options.label: C
options.text: Neither the direction nor the magnitude of its velocity changes.
options.rationale: A perpendicular force is still a force, so the direction of motion must change even though the speed does not.

options.label: D
options.text: The magnitude of its velocity changes but the direction does not.
options.rationale: The opposite of the correct answer; a force perpendicular to the velocity can only turn the particle, never speed it up or slow it down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles, both moving at the same speed. What is the ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to the radius of the proton's path?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The radius is $mv/(qB)$; an alpha particle has four times the proton's mass and twice its charge, so its radius is four halves, that is two, times as large.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This inverts the ratio, dividing the mass factor by the charge factor the wrong way round.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This uses the mass ratio alone and ignores that the alpha particle also carries twice the charge, which partly offsets its greater inertia.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This would follow only if the mass-to-charge ratios were equal, which they are not for these two particles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles, this time with the same kinetic energy. What is the ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to the radius of the proton's path?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Writing the radius as the square root of $2mK$ divided by $qB$, the alpha particle's mass advantage of four is square-rooted to two and exactly cancelled by its charge factor of two, so the radii are equal.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the answer for equal speeds rather than equal kinetic energies, where the square root from the energy expression does not appear.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This applies the charge factor but forgets the square root on the mass, so the mass advantage is undercounted by a factor of two.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This uses the mass ratio on its own, ignoring both the square root and the doubled charge of the alpha particle.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude $B$. What is the period of its motion?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The radius is $mv/(qB)$ and the period is the circumference divided by the speed, so the speed cancels and the period depends only on the mass, charge and field.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the frequency of the motion rather than the period; the two are reciprocals and the distinction is a single inversion.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This inverts the mass-to-charge ratio inside the expression, placing the charge and field in the numerator where the mass belongs.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This places the field strength in the numerator; since a stronger field bends the path more tightly, the period should shorten, not lengthen.

parts.label: e
parts.text: In a cyclotron, a charged particle is accelerated each time it crosses the gap between the two dees. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The magnetic field does no work on the particle; the increase in kinetic energy comes from the electric field in the gap.
options.rationale: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and so can only bend the path, while the electric field in the gap acts along the motion and does the accelerating.

options.label: B
options.text: The magnetic field increases the kinetic energy of the particle during each half-turn.
options.rationale: A force perpendicular to the velocity does no work, so the magnetic field cannot change the kinetic energy however strong it is.

options.label: C
options.text: The time for each half-turn increases as the particle gains speed.
options.rationale: The period is $2\pi m/(qB)$ and is independent of speed, which is precisely why a fixed-frequency alternating voltage can keep accelerating the particle.

options.label: D
options.text: The radius of the path is independent of the speed of the particle.
options.rationale: The radius is proportional to the speed, which is why the particle spirals outwards as it is accelerated rather than retracing the same circle.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** The magnetic force is $q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$, which is perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}$ by construction, so it does no work and cannot change the speed; it only turns the velocity, producing circular motion. **(A1)** Every other option in this item attributes some change in speed to the field.

**(b) A.** Setting $qvB=mv^{2}/r$ gives $r=mv/(qB)$. An alpha particle has mass $4m_{p}$ and charge $2e$, so $r_{\alpha}/r_{p}=(4/1)\times(1/2)=2$. **(A1)** C, at $4$, is the mass ratio with the charge forgotten.

**(c) A.** Now the speed is not common, so write $r=\sqrt{2mK}/(qB)$. Then $r_{\alpha}/r_{p}=\sqrt{4}\times(1/2)=2\times0.5=1$: the paths have the same radius. **(A1)** The contrast with (b) is the whole point of the pair, and B is the answer to the previous question rather than this one.

**(d) A.** $T=2\pi r/v$ with $r=mv/(qB)$ gives $T=2\pi m/(qB)$; the speed cancels, so the period does not depend on how fast the particle is moving. **(A1)** B is the reciprocal, the cyclotron frequency, and is the commonest slip here.

**(e) A.** The magnetic field bends the path and fixes the period; only the electric field in the gap can change the kinetic energy, because only it has a component along the velocity. **(A1)** C is wrong for a reason worth stating explicitly: the period is independent of speed, which is what makes the cyclotron work at a fixed frequency at all.
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per question, no negative marking. (a) Accept any wording that separates the change of direction from the constancy of speed. (b) and (c) are a pair and should be marked together in the sense that a candidate who gives the same answer to both has almost certainly not noticed that the controlled quantity changed; accept $2$ and $1$ respectively, and note that an alpha particle is a helium nucleus with mass number four and charge $+2e$. (d) Accept the expression in any equivalent form; a candidate who writes the frequency instead of the period has inverted the quantity and earns nothing unless the inversion is clearly a slip in labelling. (e) Accept any statement that identifies the electric field as the source of the energy gain; credit should not be withheld from a candidate who adds correctly that the magnetic field is what keeps the particle returning to the gap. A candidate who claims that the magnetic field accelerates the particle has misunderstood the direction of the force and should not be credited even if the rest of the description is accurate.
questions.explanation:
This cluster is built on a single fact and its consequences: the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. Once that is understood, (a) is immediate, (e) follows, and the speed-independence of the period in (d) is a one-line consequence rather than a formula to be memorised. The distractors are all what you get by treating the magnetic field as though it could speed a particle up or slow it down.

The pair (b) and (c) is the heart of the cluster and is deliberately constructed so that the same two particles give different answers depending on which quantity is held fixed. At equal speed the radius scales as $m/q$, giving a factor of two in favour of the alpha particle. At equal kinetic energy the radius scales as $\sqrt{m}/q$, and the square root turns the mass factor of four into a factor of two that exactly cancels the doubled charge, so the radii are equal. A student who has memorised one of these expressions and applies it to both questions gets one right and one wrong, and a student who re-derives the radius from whichever quantity is stated as common gets both right. That is exactly the discrimination the cluster is designed to make, and it is why the two items are placed next to each other with only the controlled quantity changed.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. Items (b) and (c) were designed as a deliberate minimal pair differing only in the controlled quantity, and the remaining distractors were built from the recurring error of treating the magnetic force as capable of doing work.

verification.method: Every key and every distractor recomputed in Python to full precision; each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error rather than a nearby number.
solution_skeleton: note that the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and so does no work
equate the magnetic force to the centripetal requirement to obtain the path radius
express the radius in terms of the quantity the question holds constant
divide the circumference by the speed so that the speed cancels to give the period
identify which field does work on the particle in an accelerator
